answer: The busiest time I can remember was about a year ago, and I still feel slightly tired just thinking about it. A period when I was extraordinarily busy was during the final weeks before a major deadline at work, which happened to coincide with a family event. At the consultancy, it was the peak of the application season, when lots of students were trying to submit their university applications at once, and at the same time my cousin was getting married in our ancestral village. I found myself juggling long working hours with preparations at home, and there simply were not enough hours in the day. My schedule was absolutely [[relentless]]; I would wake early, work through lunch and often continue late into the night. Then at weekends I travelled to the village to help with the arrangements for the wedding. At times it felt genuinely [[overwhelming]], and I worried I might [[drop the ball]] on something important. What got me through was staying organised, making detailed lists and [[prioritising ruthlessly]]. Somehow I managed to meet the deadline and see the family event through successfully. As for how I felt, I was exhausted but also quietly proud. Looking back, it taught me a great deal about managing pressure, and I discovered I was more [[capable]] under stress than I had thought. Honestly, while I would not want to repeat it too often, it was a valuable lesson in resilience and time management.

followUps.q: How do you usually relax after a busy period?
followUps.answer: I like to take a long walk by the Jamuna in the evening, or just sit at home with a cup of tea and a book. After that busy month, I mostly caught up on sleep.

followUps.q: Do you think people are busier now than in the past?
followUps.answer: I think so. My father worked hard, but his work mostly stayed at the shop. Now phones mean work follows us home, so it is much harder to switch off completely.

note: Specified application season and a cousin's wedding in the ancestral village; marked 'drop the ball' and 'prioritising ruthlessly' instead of plain 'organised'.
